hints: Reverse the splitting process: merge final pieces into the original stick.
A merge costs the combined length of its two pieces.
Repeatedly merge the two shortest pieces, as in Huffman coding.
analogy: Short pieces are combined early so their lengths are charged at deeper levels instead of making large pieces pay repeatedly.
example: For lengths 2,3,5, merge 2+3 at cost 5, then 5+5 at cost 10, for total 15.
algorithm: Put all target lengths into a min-heap. Repeatedly remove the two smallest, add their sum to the answer, and insert the sum. When one length remains, print the accumulated cost; with one piece the answer is zero. Use wide integers.
correctness: In an optimal binary merge tree, two smallest leaves can be placed as deepest siblings without increasing cost. Merging them reduces the problem to an optimal smaller instance, establishing the greedy rule.
complexity: For n pieces, O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
